title: The services page a consumer brand actually needs
metaTitle: The menu a consumer brand needs
excerpt: List what a shopper can get, in words they would use in a shop. Each offer needs an outcome, a boundary, and a next step that shows the product.
alt: Pale blue and orange ink swirls on a white ground. A surface with a few clear gestures, which is how a product menu should read.
caption: Pale blue and orange ink swirls on a white ground. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What counts as an offer on a brand menu?
faqs.answer: Something a person can receive or book: the mug, the refill, the repair, the gift set. Craft, community, and ritual can be true and still fail as headings. Fold a true claim into the offer it changes, such as a replaceable sole on the shoe.

faqs.question: What should each block include?
faqs.answer: The outcome in physical terms, the boundary, and a way to see the product. The refill does not include the bottle. The made-to-order piece has a lead time and a return rule. Say those edges in the block, in the same type as the promise.

faqs.question: How do you know the nouns work?
faqs.answer: Read the headings aloud with the pictures hidden. A stranger should be able to point at the offer they want. If they need the photograph to guess, the words are still a mood, and another shoot will not fix them.

sources.title: Influencing Title Links in Google Search

markdown:
A consumer brand services page should list what a shopper can actually get, in words they would use in a shop. Each offer needs an outcome, a boundary, and a next step: see the product. A grid of vague capabilities, "craft," "community," "ritual," does not help someone choose.

The page is a menu of goods and the few services around them. The object, the refill, the made-to-order piece, the care, the gift wrap. If a line could sit on any brand's homepage, it is not yet an offer.

## Name the offers the way a shopper speaks

People say mug, jacket, refill, gift set, repair, swatch. Use those words as the headings. Internal collection codes and seasonal poetry can sit in a smaller line. The heading has to be something a stranger can repeat to a friend.

Google's guidance on [title links](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) asks for descriptive titles and warns that boilerplate makes pages impossible to tell apart. A services or shop menu has the same duty. "The edit," "The world," and "The story" are interchangeable. "Mugs," "Refills," and "Repairs" are not. If you need poetry, put it after the noun, not instead of the noun.

One page can hold the menu when you have a handful of offers. Give an offer its own page when it has its own pictures, its own price shape, and its own rules, such as made-to-order with a lead time. The menu page still has to stand alone. A shopper should know which door is theirs before they click.

Down the Cove is a public example of a brand shop rebuilt with a point of view: ecommerce restructure, migration, and redesign. The menu lesson is editorial. A catalog can be grouped so a new shopper sees distinct offers, with the object intact. Wabisabi, a calm brand site, is a reminder that the menu can be quiet and still be specific. Neither project is a template. Both show that naming can stay plain.

## Outcome: what the person has after they buy

Each block should say what arrives or what changes. A mug that holds 300 ml and fits under a standard machine. A jacket cut for layering, with the pockets described. A refill that assumes you already own the bottle. A repair that returns the same object, cleaned and resoles, in a stated number of weeks.

The outcome is physical. "Elevate your morning" can be deleted without losing information. "A cup you can put in the dishwasher, with a glaze that crazes over time" cannot. The second sentence tells a shopper whether they want that life. Some will. Some will want a mug that stays pristine. Both deserve a clear outcome so they can sort themselves.

If the offer is a set, say what the set is for. A gift set with the object, a note card, and a pouch. A starter set with the thing and the first refill. People buy sets when the outcome is "I do not have to choose." Write that. Leave the mystery for the unboxing, not for the menu.

Level and taste belong here too. A scent described as smoke and leather will disappoint someone who wanted fresh cotton. A denim described as rigid will disappoint someone who wanted softness on day one. The disappointment is a boundary failure you can prevent with a sentence.

## Boundary: what this offer will not do

Every offer needs an edge. The refill does not include the bottle. The repair does not include a lost button you cannot match. The made-to-order cloth is cut for you and cannot be returned as if it were stock. The glaze varies, and the photograph is one example. Say the edge in the block, in the same type as the outcome, so it is part of the offer.

A boundary protects the brand from promises the workshop cannot keep. If you cannot engrave this season, the menu should not show engraving. If international shipping is paused, say so on the block that people try to send abroad. A hidden limit becomes a support queue. A printed limit becomes a confident shop.

Where two offers overlap, say how to choose. Buy the starter if you are new. Buy the refill if you already have the bottle. Buy the set if this is a gift and you want the pouch. That is a path. Six identical cards with no path are a moodboard.

Care can be its own offer when you mean it. A resoling service. A cleaning guide that is actually a product decision, such as "do not soak." Put the guide near the object. A floating "services" page that never links to the thing being serviced is how care becomes abstract. The next step pulls it back to the product.

## The next step is to see the product

End each block with the product, in a label a shopper understands. See the mug. See the jacket. Start a repair. The destination is the object, the set, or the form that begins that specific service, with the price shape visible. "Learn more" is a stall if the next page is another essay.

One primary action per block. A secondary line can link care instructions or sizing. If every card has four buttons, the menu is a directory of the website, not a directory of the goods. The person who does not know you yet needs the product.

Repeat a clear action at the bottom for the shopper who read the whole menu. Same verbs. If they are still unsure, point them at the single hero object from the homepage, the one you would put in their hand first. A menu that refuses to recommend is an abdication. You know the range better than they do. Recommend the ordinary starting point, and let the rest of the menu be the alternative.

Photographs on the menu should be the products, shot to the same brief. One crop, one ground, the object large enough to name. A different mood for every card tells the shopper the offers come from different brands. You are one brand. The menu should look like one room.

## Cut the capability grid

Brand sites copy agency grids when they are nervous. Craft. Community. Sustainability. Heritage. Those words can be true and still be useless as a menu. Fold any true claim into the offer it changes. "Repairable sole" belongs on the shoe. "Refillable" belongs on the bottle. A claim with nowhere to land is a poster.

Read only the headings aloud. If a shopper could point at one and say "that one," the menu works. If they would still need to ask what you sell, the headings are still a manifesto. Fix the nouns.

Watch for offers that exist because a template had six slots. A journal card, a playlist card, a loyalty card with no program behind it. Empty slots make the real objects look like content. Publish the things you can ship or service this month. Add a card when the workshop can fulfill it.

Keep the top of the page short. One sentence on who the goods are for, then the menu. The about story can wait. A shopper who wants the maker will look for people after they trust the object. Reversing that order is how the menu becomes a brochure.

## How the menu stays true

Seasonal offers should carry their season and then leave. A card for a sold-out collaboration, with no note and no alternative, trains people to distrust the next card. Mark the end, or remove the card and keep the story on a proof page if the story is still useful.

Someone has to own the menu. Often it is the same person who owns the product page. When a material changes, the outcome sentence changes. When a repair service pauses, the block pauses. A Hanabi-built marketing or shop front can keep this as editable content. The stack the studio ships is Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind. The reason it matters is dull and important: the menu has to change when the workshop changes, without a new design project.

Prices on the menu, if you show them, must be the same prices as the product page. One source. A teaser price that is "from" a number you cannot find on the next page is a boundary violation. Either print the real from-range or wait until the product page.

Read the menu to someone who has never seen the range, with the pictures hidden. If they can still point at the offer they want from the words alone, the nouns are doing the work. If they need the pictures to guess, the headings are still mood. Fix the words before you commission another photograph. The photograph should confirm the noun, not rescue it.

## Who makes the thing

A clear menu raises a human question. Who stands behind the object, and why should a stranger care. Answer with the people and the method that change the decision to see the product. Skip the origin myth unless it changes that decision. That is [how a consumer brand should write an about page](/blog/how-a-consumer-brand-should-write-an-about-page).

If the menu is the piece you want help editing, start with [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) and see how brand shops group the goods. Then bring your real list, including the offers you are not ready to ship.
